details.label: Discussion
details.text: An isolated thunderstorm is evolving along the surface trough/wind shift in central SD, with additional agitated boundary-layer cumulus nearby. Steep midlevel lapse rates atop an increasingly unstable PBL is yielding moderate surface-based buoyancy, which combined with an elongating/straight hodograph (around 40 kt of effective shear), will support splitting supercells and small organized clusters. The primary concern will be large to very large hail and locally severe wind gusts. It is unclear how many storms will develop, given somewhat modest large-scale forcing for ascent and some lingering inhibition at the base of the EML. However, given the favorable environment, trends are being monitored and a watch is at least being considered

details.label: Summary
details.text: The threat for at least isolated severe storms capable of severe wind gusts up to 65-80 mph and large hail potentially up to two inches is expected to increase late this afternoon through this evening. A watch is possible

details.label: Discussion
details.text: Visible satellite imagery shows a growing cumulus field from Ogallala north toward Merriman in western NE, in the vicinity of a surface trough. Additional, more elevated convection is noted along the SD-NE border, near Pine Ridge. The 18Z North Platte sounding sampled the presence of an EML with considerable capping for surface-based parcels. Since that observation, surface temperatures have warmed through the 80s into lower 90s, effectively reducing the amount of convective inhibition. Forcing for ascent associated with a subtle short-wave trough currently moving through eastern WY in conjunction with continued daytime heating is expected locally erode the cap such that isolated thunderstorm development will become increasingly likely within the next 1-3 hours along the surface trough and/or cool front moving into the region from the north. The presence of steep low/mid-level lapse rates and a vertically veering wind profile with 30-35 kt of deep-layer shear will support organized storm modes, including supercells with an associated risk for large hail, potentially up to two inches and locally severe wind gusts. Latest time-lagged HRRR and RRFS guidance suggests that a more robust damaging wind threat could materialize this evening as storms merge into clusters, at which point gusts up to 65-80 mph would become more likely
